key_insight: Different language models independently learn periodic numeric features with dominant periods T = 2, 5, 10, but only some models arrange those features into geometrically separable patterns that support linear classification of numbers mod-T.
problem_solved: Explains why different architectures trained on the same natural text encode number information similarly in the frequency domain yet differ in whether that information is directly usable by simple linear probes.
method: Empirical survey of multiple architectures (Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, classical word embeddings) trained on natural text to extract number-related representations.
Fourier-domain analysis to identify dominant periodic components (spikes at T = 2, 5, 10) in learned features.

Geometric/separability tests and linear-probe experiments to determine which models produce features that are linearly classifiable mod‑T, plus analysis linking outcomes to architectural/training factors.
impact: Clarifies how inductive biases of architectures affect whether numeracy is encoded in a directly usable form, informing model selection, probe design, and interpretability efforts for arithmetic and numeracy-sensitive tasks.
visual_elements: Fourier spectrum plot showing spikes at periods T = 2, 5, 10 for multiple models (overlaid lines or small multiples).
Side-by-side 2D embedding scatter (PCA/t-SNE) comparing geometrically separable vs non-separable features with linear decision boundaries drawn.
Bar chart/table summarizing which architectures yield linear separability for each T.
Simple schematic illustrating the two-tier hierarchy: (1) universal Fourier-periodic features, (2) model-dependent geometric arrangement enabling linear probes.
paper_title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
paper_authors: Deqing Fu, Tianyi Zhou, Mikhail Belkin, Vatsal Sharan, Robin Jia
